paragraphs: Among the many advantages promised by a well-constructed Union, none deserves to be explained more carefully than its tendency to break and control the violence of faction. The friend of popular governments is never so alarmed for their character and fate as when he considers their tendency toward this dangerous vice. He will therefore be sure to value any plan that offers a proper cure for it without violating the principles to which he is attached. Instability, injustice and confusion in the public councils have in truth been the mortal diseases of which popular governments have everywhere perished. They also remain the favorite and fruitful themes from which the adversaries of liberty draw their most plausible speeches. The valuable improvements that the American constitutions have made on the popular models, ancient and modern, cannot be admired too much. But it would be unwarranted partiality to contend that they have guarded as effectively against danger on this side as was wished and expected. Complaints are heard everywhere from our most thoughtful and virtuous citizens, equally friends of public and private faith and of public and personal liberty. They say that our governments are too unstable, that the public good is disregarded in the conflicts of rival parties, and that measures are too often decided not by the rules of justice and the rights of the minority but by the superior force of an interested and overbearing majority. However anxiously we may wish that these complaints had no foundation, the evidence of known facts will not let us deny that they are true to some degree. An honest review of our situation will show, indeed, that some of the distresses we suffer have been wrongly blamed on the way our governments operate. But it will show at the same time that other causes cannot alone account for many of our heaviest misfortunes, and particularly for that prevailing and increasing distrust of public engagements, and alarm for private rights, which are echoed from one end of the continent to the other. These must be chiefly, if not wholly, the effects of the unsteadiness and injustice with which a factional spirit has tainted our public administrations.

By a faction, I understand a number of citizens, whether amounting to a majority or a minority of the whole, who are united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adverse to the rights of other citizens, or to the permanent and aggregate interests of the community.
There are two methods of curing the harms of faction. One is to remove its causes. The other is to control its effects.

Its causes, in turn, can be removed in two ways. One is to destroy the liberty that faction needs in order to exist. The other is to give every citizen the same opinions, the same passions and the same interests.

It could never be said more truly of any remedy than of the first, that it was worse than the disease. Liberty is to faction what air is to fire: a nourishment without which it instantly dies. But it would be no less foolish to abolish liberty, which is essential to political life, because it feeds faction, than to wish for the destruction of air, which is essential to animal life, because it gives fire its destructive power.

The second remedy is as impracticable as the first would be unwise. As long as human reason remains fallible, and man is at liberty to use it, different opinions will be formed. As long as a connection remains between his reason and his self-love, his opinions and his passions will influence each other, and the former will be objects to which the latter attach themselves. The diversity in the faculties of men, from which the rights of property originate, is just as insuperable an obstacle to uniformity of interests. The protection of these faculties is the first object of government. From the protection of different and unequal faculties for acquiring property, the possession of different degrees and kinds of property immediately follows. And from the influence of these on the views and feelings of their respective owners comes a division of society into different interests and parties.

The latent causes of faction are thus sown in the nature of man, and we see them everywhere brought into different degrees of activity according to the different circumstances of civil society. A zeal for different opinions about religion, about government and about many other points, of speculation as well as of practice; an attachment to different leaders ambitiously contending for pre-eminence and power, or to persons of other kinds whose fortunes have engaged the human passions: these have in turn divided mankind into parties, inflamed them with mutual animosity, and made them far more disposed to vex and oppress each other than to cooperate for their common good. So strong is this tendency of mankind to fall into mutual animosities that, where no real occasion presents itself, the most frivolous and fanciful distinctions have been enough to kindle their unfriendly passions and excite their most violent conflicts. But the most common and lasting source of factions has been the various and unequal distribution of property. Those who hold property and those who have none have always formed distinct interests in society. Creditors and debtors are divided in a similar way. A landed interest, a manufacturing interest, a mercantile interest, a moneyed interest, with many lesser interests, grow up of necessity in civilized nations and divide them into different classes, moved by different views and feelings. The regulation of these various and conflicting interests is the principal task of modern legislation, and it brings the spirit of party and faction into the necessary and ordinary operations of government.

No man is allowed to be a judge in his own cause, because his interest would certainly bias his judgment and, not improbably, corrupt his integrity. With equal reason, indeed with greater, a body of men is unfit to be judge and party at the same time. Yet what are many of the most important acts of legislation but so many judicial decisions, concerning not the rights of single persons but the rights of large bodies of citizens? And what are the different classes of legislators but advocates and parties to the causes they decide? Is a law proposed concerning private debts? It is a question in which the creditors are parties on one side and the debtors on the other. Justice ought to hold the balance between them. Yet the parties are, and must be, themselves the judges, and the most numerous party, or in other words the most powerful faction, must be expected to prevail. Shall domestic manufactures be encouraged, and to what degree, by restrictions on foreign manufactures? These are questions that the landed and the manufacturing classes would decide differently, and probably neither with sole regard to justice and the public good. The apportionment of taxes on the various kinds of property is an act that seems to require the most exact impartiality. Yet there is perhaps no legislative act in which a dominant party has greater opportunity and temptation to trample on the rules of justice. Every shilling with which they overburden the smaller number is a shilling saved to their own pockets.

It is useless to say that enlightened statesmen will be able to reconcile these clashing interests and make them all serve the public good. Enlightened statesmen will not always be at the helm. And in many cases such a reconciliation cannot be made at all without weighing indirect and distant considerations, which will seldom outweigh the immediate interest a party may have in ignoring the rights of others or the good of the whole.
The conclusion we are brought to is that the CAUSES of faction cannot be removed, and that relief is to be sought only in means of controlling its EFFECTS.

If a faction is less than a majority, the republican principle supplies the relief: the majority can defeat the faction's sinister aims by a regular vote. The faction may obstruct the administration and may throw the society into convulsions, but it cannot carry out its violence and disguise it under the forms of the Constitution. When a majority is part of a faction, however, the form of popular government lets it sacrifice both the public good and the rights of other citizens to its ruling passion or interest. To secure the public good and private rights against the danger of such a faction, while preserving the spirit and the form of popular government, is therefore the great object of our inquiry. Let me add that it is the great desideratum by which this form of government can be rescued from the disgrace it has suffered for so long and be recommended to the esteem and adoption of mankind.

By what means can this object be attained? Evidently by one of only two means. Either the same passion or interest must be prevented from existing in a majority at the same time, or the majority, having such a shared passion or interest, must be made unable, by their number and local situation, to act together and carry out schemes of oppression. If impulse and opportunity are allowed to coincide, we know well that neither moral nor religious motives can be relied on as an adequate control. They are not found to control the injustice and violence of individuals, and they lose their effectiveness in proportion to the number of people combined, that is, in proportion as their effectiveness becomes necessary.

From this view of the subject we may conclude that a pure democracy, by which I mean a society consisting of a small number of citizens who assemble and administer the government in person, can offer no cure for the harms of faction. In almost every case, a majority of the whole will feel a common passion or interest. The form of government itself produces communication and concert, and nothing checks the temptation to sacrifice the weaker party or an unpopular individual. This is why such democracies have always been spectacles of turbulence and contention, have always been incompatible with personal security and the rights of property, and have generally been as short in life as they have been violent in death. Theoretical politicians who have championed this kind of government have mistakenly supposed that if mankind were made perfectly equal in political rights, people would at the same time become perfectly equal and alike in their possessions, opinions and passions.

A republic, by which I mean a government in which the scheme of representation takes place, opens a different prospect and promises the cure we seek. Let us examine how it differs from pure democracy, and we shall understand both the nature of the cure and the effectiveness it must draw from the Union.

The two great points of difference between a democracy and a republic are these: first, in the latter the government is delegated to a small number of citizens elected by the rest; second, the latter can be extended over a greater number of citizens and a greater sphere of country.

The effect of the first difference is, on the one hand, to refine and enlarge the public views by passing them through the medium of a chosen body of citizens. Their wisdom may best discern the true interest of their country, and their patriotism and love of justice will be least likely to sacrifice it to temporary or biased considerations. Under such an arrangement it may well happen that the public voice, expressed by the representatives of the people, will be more in line with the public good than if the people themselves, convened for the purpose, expressed it. On the other hand, the effect may be reversed. Men of factional temperament, local prejudices or sinister designs may, by intrigue, corruption or other means, first win the votes and then betray the interests of the people. The question that results is whether small or extensive republics are more favorable to the election of proper guardians of the public welfare. Two obvious considerations clearly decide it in favor of the latter.

In the first place, it is to be remarked that however small the republic may be, the representatives must be raised to a certain number in order to guard against the cabals of a few; and that however large it may be, they must be limited to a certain number in order to guard against the confusion of a multitude. Hence the number of representatives in the two cases is not in proportion to the number of their constituents, and is proportionally greater in the small republic. It follows that if the proportion of fit characters is no smaller in the large republic than in the small one, the former will offer a greater choice and consequently a greater probability of a fit choice.

In the next place, since each representative will be chosen by a greater number of citizens in the large republic than in the small one, it will be more difficult for unworthy candidates to practice with success the vicious arts by which elections are too often won. And since the votes of the people will be freer, they will be more likely to center on men who have the most attractive merit and the most widespread and established characters.

It must be confessed that in this, as in most other cases, there is a mean, on both sides of which problems will be found. By enlarging the number of electors too much, you make the representative too little acquainted with all their local circumstances and lesser interests. By reducing it too much, you make him unduly attached to these, and too little fit to understand and pursue great and national objects. The federal Constitution forms a happy combination in this respect: the great and aggregate interests are referred to the national legislature, the local and particular to the State legislatures.

The other difference is that a republic can embrace a greater number of citizens and a greater extent of territory than a democracy can. This is the circumstance that chiefly makes factional combinations less to be feared in a republic than in a democracy. The smaller the society, the fewer distinct parties and interests it probably contains. The fewer the distinct parties and interests, the more often a majority will belong to the same party. And the fewer the individuals who make up a majority, and the smaller the area they occupy, the more easily they will concert and carry out their plans of oppression. Extend the sphere and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests. You make it less probable that a majority of the whole will have a common motive to invade the rights of other citizens. And if such a motive does exist, it will be harder for all who feel it to discover their own strength and act together. Among other obstacles, it may be noted that where people are conscious of unjust or dishonorable purposes, distrust always restrains communication, in proportion to the number whose agreement is needed.

It is therefore clear that the advantage a republic has over a democracy in controlling the effects of faction is also the advantage of a large republic over a small one, and of the Union over the States that compose it. Does the advantage lie in putting in place representatives whose enlightened views and virtuous feelings raise them above local prejudices and schemes of injustice? No one will deny that the representation of the Union will be most likely to have these necessary qualities. Does it lie in the greater security that a greater variety of parties gives against any one party being able to outnumber and oppress the rest? The greater variety of parties within the Union increases that security equally. Does it lie, finally, in the greater obstacles to the concert and accomplishment of the secret wishes of an unjust and interested majority? Here again the extent of the Union gives it the most obvious advantage.

Factional leaders may kindle a flame in their own States, but they will be unable to spread a general fire through the other States. A religious sect may degenerate into a political faction in one part of the Confederacy, but the variety of sects scattered over the whole of it must protect the national councils from any danger from that source. A rage for paper money, for abolishing debts, for an equal division of property, or for any other improper or wicked project will be less likely to spread through the whole body of the Union than through one member of it, in the same proportion as such a sickness is more likely to infect a single county or district than an entire State.

In the extent and proper structure of the Union, then, we see a republican remedy for the diseases most common in republican government. The more pleasure and pride we take in being republicans, the more zeal we ought to show in cherishing the spirit and supporting the character of Federalists.
